commitResults.messageTitle: Add saving and loading of the task list
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list lives only in memory, so everything the user enters is
lost when the program exits.

Let's write the list to data/saved.txt whenever it changes, and read it
back at start-up. One line holds one task, as
"type | marked | text | by/from | to". The fields hold the text the user
typed, not the decorated display form, because Level-8 replaces the time
fields with real dates and a display-based format would have to be
rewritten then. A | inside a field is written as \| so that it cannot be
mistaken for a separator on the way back in.

A failed write now raises TaskSaveException, and the command that
triggered it undoes its own change before reporting. The list on screen
therefore always matches the file, and the user can retry the command
without creating a duplicate.

A save file with any line that does not match the format is deleted and
reported at start-up. A partly loaded agenda hides what is missing,
which is worse for the user than starting empty.

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace free-text times with real dates
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and event times are plain text, so the program cannot order
them, compare them, or tell a real date from a typing mistake.

Let's store both as java.time.LocalDateTime. The user gives a date,
2019-10-15, or a date and a time, 2019-10-15 1800. A date on its own
takes a default: midnight for a deadline, and 23:59 for an event's end,
so that a whole-day event covers the whole day.

Three formats now exist and are deliberately different. The user types
yyyy-MM-dd, the save file holds the ISO form, and the display shows
MMM dd yyyy, HH:mm. Only this program reads the file, so it keeps the
machine form rather than either human one. Parsing is strict, so
2019-02-30 is an error rather than being moved to the end of the month,
and DateFormatException keeps DateTimeParseException away from the user.

An event that ends before it starts is checkable for the first time and
now raises EventFormatException. A save file from before this change
holds text such as "June 6th", which no longer parses; the existing rule
deletes it, and the message now says so in those words.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract user interaction into a Ui class
commitResults.messageBody:
Every print statement, and the only read from the keyboard, sits in
GudGoi alongside the task list, the command dispatch and the file
handling. A-MoreOOP asks for those responsibilities to be separated.
The console is the easiest one to lift out first, because nothing else
in the program depends on how a response looks.

Let's move the banner, the greeting, the farewell, the divider, the
response printer and readCommand into a new Ui class, and give GudGoi a
Ui to speak through. Nothing outside Ui now writes to the screen or
reads from the keyboard, so a later move to a window rather than a
console touches one class.

The change preserves behaviour. The build before and the build after
were run over six scenarios covering the happy path, every error
message, escaped separators, end of input, an empty list and a corrupt
save file. Both stdout and the save file came out identical, byte for
byte.

Ui is an ordinary object rather than a set of static methods, because
GudGoi gains a constructor in a later step of A-MoreOOP and will hold it
as a field. It is reached through a static field here only because
GudGoi itself is still static.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract file handling into a Storage class
commitResults.messageBody:
GudGoi still owns the save file: the path, the line format, when to
write, and what to say when a file cannot be read. A-MoreOOP asks for
storage to be a responsibility of its own, and it is the next easiest to
lift because only five call sites reach it.

Let's move SAVE_PATH, save, load, parseSavedTask, unescape and
discardCorruptFile into a Storage class built from a file path.

Storage does not print. A file it cannot read raises the new
TaskLoadException, a file it cannot write raises TaskSaveException, and
the caller decides how the user hears about it. That is the part that
matters: it lets one class serve a console now and a window at Level-10,
and it follows the shape the A-MoreOOP example shows, where the main
class catches a load failure and asks the Ui to report it.

load returns the tasks rather than filling the list in place, because
TaskList owns that list two increments from now, and a Storage that
reached into it would have to be written twice.

Storage takes a Path rather than the String of the example, because a
Path already carries the separator the host system uses.

The change preserves behaviour. The build before and the build after
were run over seven scenarios, including a corrupt file that has to be
deleted and a read-only file whose failure has to be reported and
undone. Both stdout and the save file came out identical, byte for byte.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract the task list into a TaskList class
commitResults.messageBody:
GudGoi holds the ArrayList and every command reaches into it directly.
Several methods each remember that the user counts from 1 while the
list indexes from 0, so the same correction is written more than once.

Let's move the list into a TaskList class. Positions counted from 1 are
the language it speaks, and it is the only code that has to know about
the offset.

The bounds check moves with the list, because only the list knows how
long it is. Reading the number out of the command text does not: that is
parsing, and it stays behind as parsePosition until the parser exists.
So taskAt becomes two steps that raise the same two Exceptions in the
same order as before.

TaskList neither saves nor prints, for the reason Storage does not
print. GudGoi still decides the order: change the list, ask Storage to
write it, undo the change if the write failed, then ask Ui to say what
happened. insert and removeLast exist for that undo and for nothing
else, which their comments say.

asList hands out a read-only view. Storage and the numbered listing only
read, and routing every change through the methods keeps this class the
one place that decides what the agenda holds.

The tasks field is no longer final, because start-up now replaces it
with a list built from what storage returned rather than filling an
empty one.

The change preserves behaviour. The build before and the build after
were run over eight scenarios, including stale task numbers after a
delete, deleting down to an empty list, and a read-only file that forces
an add, a mark, an unmark and a delete each to be undone. Both stdout
and the save file came out identical, byte for byte.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract command reading into a Parser class
commitResults.messageBody:
GudGoi still reads the command text: splitting a line into a verb and
its arguments, finding /by, /from and /to, reading dates, and reading
task numbers. That is the last of the four responsibilities A-MoreOOP
names, and the only one still mixed into the class that answers
commands.

Let's move all of it into a Parser, and let it return the finished task.

That choice is the one worth arguing. A parser could instead return the
pieces it found and leave GudGoi to build the task, but the pieces
differ per command, so each would need a carrier type that exists only
to be unpacked one line later. Turning "deadline read book /by
2019-10-15" into a Deadline is what making sense of the command means.
The stretch goal goes further, to a Command object per verb, which is
more than the minimal target asks for.

Three methods disappear as a result. addTodo, addDeadline and addEvent
each became a single call once the reading moved out, so the dispatch
calls the parser directly instead. GudGoi is now 224 lines, from 616
before this week's first extraction, and holds only the order of the
steps: change the list, write it, undo the change if the write failed,
then say what happened.

Parser's methods are static, because parsing remembers nothing between
one command and the next, so an instance would carry no state. The cost
is that a different parser cannot be substituted without changing the
callers.

mark, unmark and deleteTask now declare GudGoiException rather than
naming three Exception types each. Which type a bad argument raises
stopped being their business when the parsing moved out.

The change preserves behaviour. The build before and the build after
were run over ten scenarios, including command words in the wrong case,
delimiters with no space around them, a repeated /by, an argument that
looks like a delimiter, leap years, and an event whose end falls before
its start. Both stdout and the save file came out identical, byte for
byte.

commitResults.messageTitle: Turn GudGoi into an object with a constructor
commitResults.messageBody:
The four classes A-MoreOOP asks for now exist, but GudGoi still reaches
them through static fields, and every method it owns is static too. That
was a stopgap while the extractions ran, and three comments say so.

Let's give the class a constructor that takes the save path, make ui,
storage and tasks ordinary fields, move the session into run(), and
leave main as the one line that starts it. Only main is static now.

The example in the spec loads the file inside the constructor. This does
not, and the difference is deliberate. Loading can fail, and the failure
has to be reported, so a constructor that loads is a constructor that
prints, and it prints before the greeting. A user told their save file
was deleted before the bot has said hello does not know who is talking.
The constructor here only wires the parts together, and cannot fail;
run() greets first and reads the file second.

That also keeps the output in the order it has always been, which is
what let this commit be checked the same way as the four before it.

The change preserves behaviour. The build before and the build after
were run over ten scenarios, and both stdout and the save file came out
identical, byte for byte.

The coding standard check now reports nothing across every source file.
The two remaining complaints were ui and storage, which were static
final with lower-case names, and both are ordinary fields as of this
commit.

commitResults.messageTitle: chore: Add the commit skill and the week 3 plan
commitResults.messageBody:
Two of the three repository skills were already tracked. The checks I
run before every commit lived only in the conversation, so they were
followed from memory and one commit went in with an unwrapped message
body before the slip was noticed and amended.

Let's keep them in the repository, next to the other skills.

The git-commit skill holds the order of the checks: read the diff,
compile, read the coding standard, run the tests or ask for a green
light, cite the AI assistance in both the code and the README, then
write a message that follows the commit convention, and only then
branch, tag and push. Two shell scripts do the mechanical part.
check-conventions.sh reads a Java file against the se-education
intermediate standard, and check-commit-message.sh reads a message
against the Git standard. Both report suspects for a person to judge
rather than verdicts, because neither is a parser.

The week 3 plan and the roadmap now carry what the course website said
on 27 August: branches start this week, the merge commit takes the tag,
and the commit message standard applies from now on. decisions.md
records the Level-7 save format, the failure policy behind it, and why
JSON was not used.

README gains a line naming these skills as development notes generated
by Claude. They are not part of the chatbot and no code from them
reaches src, but the course asks for AI assistance to be declared, and
declaring it costs nothing.

All 19 classes sit in the default package, which the coding standard
does not allow: every class must belong to a package. A-Packages asks
for this, and it has to happen before A-Gradle, or the build settings
and the test paths both move twice.

Let's use three packages under src/main/java: gudgoi for the app and
its parts, gudgoi.task for the four task types, and gudgoi.exception
for the ten Exception types.

The split was chosen by what a later move would cost. Task and its
subclasses are named from five other files, and the Exception types are
ten classes already with more due at A-MoreErrorHandling, so both are
expensive to move later and are moved now. Ui stays beside GudGoi,
because only GudGoi names it, so moving it costs one import line. That
matters at Level-10, which brings three or four JavaFX classes with it:
gudgoi.ui is worth creating when it has something to hold, not today
when it would hold one class.

No package is created for Commands. That is the A-MoreOOP stretch goal,
which is not being taken, and an empty package waiting for a maybe is
not worth the folder.

One thing had to change beyond the move. EventFormatException shows the
two times of a rejected event, and it read Task.DISPLAY_FORMAT to do so.
That field was protected, and the Exception is not a subclass of Task,
so it only ever compiled because both were in the default package. It is
public now. A DateTimeFormatter cannot be changed once it is built, so
sharing this one hands out no control over it, and the name was already
that of a constant.

Moving DISPLAY_FORMAT to Ui would also have solved it, and would be the
larger question of where display formatting belongs. That question is
worth answering on its own at A-CodeQuality, not as a side effect of
sorting files into folders.

Every file moved with git mv, so the history follows each one, and 19
stale class files were cleared out of the source folder.

The program is now started as gudgoi.GudGoi rather than GudGoi.

The change preserves behaviour. The build before and the build after
were run over ten scenarios, and both stdout and the save file came out
identical, byte for byte.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'add-gradle-support' from the course repository
commitResults.messageBody:
The Duke repository carries a branch holding a ready Gradle setup, and
A-Gradle asks for it to be merged rather than written from scratch. It
brings build.gradle, the Gradle wrapper, and the two wrapper scripts,
and it changes no file this project already had.

The settings it arrives with suit this project: Java 25, which the
project requires, JUnit 5 ready for A-JUnit, and the shadow plugin ready
for the fat JAR in week 5. Only the names of this project have to be
filled in, which the next commit does.

The build file that arrived with the merge is the template's, so it
names seedu.duke.Duke as the class to start and duke.jar as the file to
package. Neither name exists here.

Let's set mainClass to gudgoi.GudGoi and the packaged name to
gudgoi.jar. Nothing else in the file needed changing: it already asks
for Java 25, which this project requires, it already wires JUnit 5 for
A-JUnit, and it already carries the shadow plugin for the fat JAR in
week 5.

No Java file changed in this increment, so there is no behaviour to
compare. What was checked is the build. gradlew build succeeds, gradlew
run drives the chatbot and reads the keyboard, and the packaged JAR runs
on its own.

Running through Gradle also settles a problem that has been biting.
Level-7 stores the agenda at a path relative to the folder the program
starts in, and starting it from the wrong folder had been leaving a data
directory inside the source tree. Gradle starts the program from the
project root, which is the folder the spec assumes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for parser, storage and task list
commitResults.messageBody:
The only checking this project has had is me running it by hand and
reading the output. That found real faults, but it found them once: the
knowledge lived in a terminal that has since been closed, and nothing
stops any of them coming back.

Let's turn what those runs found into tests that run on every build.

A-JUnit asks for two non-trivial methods in two classes. There are three
classes here, because the three are where a fault would actually hide.
Parser is pure text in, values out, and it holds every date and
delimiter rule. Storage is the only code that writes a file the program
must be able to read again. TaskList is the only code that knows the
user counts from 1 while a list counts from 0.

The cases are the ones that once broke or nearly broke the program:
2019-02-30, which a lenient parser would quietly move to the end of
February; 2019-02-29 against 2020-02-29; a doubled space before a time;
an event whose end falls before its start, including when both are dates
alone and the defaults decide it; a | inside a description, which would
shift every field after it on the way back in; a save file in the format
used before Level-8; and every end of the position range.

Storage writes into a folder JUnit makes and deletes for each test, so
no test can touch a real agenda or leave anything behind. Tasks are
compared by their save form, because the task types define no equals and
the save form carries everything that survives a restart.

54 tests, all passing. The test task no longer reports NO-SOURCE, so a
green build now means something it did not mean yesterday: a failing
test fails the build, which I checked by adding a deliberately wrong
assertion and watching it stop the build before removing it again.

A long agenda can only be read in full. There is no way to ask which of
it mentions a particular thing.

Let's add find, which prints the tasks whose description holds a word.

Each match keeps the number it has in the whole agenda. The example in
the spec numbers the matches from 1 instead, and that reads well until
the user acts on it: after a find that shows two results, mark 1 marks
whatever is first in the full list, which may be neither of the things
on the screen. Showing the real position means the number on the screen
is the number mark and delete accept.

The cost is that the numbers now have gaps, so a reader must not assume
they are counting from one. That seemed the smaller surprise of the two.

The search ignores case, because a person looking for a word rarely
remembers how they capitalised it, and it looks at the description only,
which is what the increment asks for. A word that matches nothing gets a
plain answer rather than an empty list under a heading that promises
matches.

An empty keyword raises FindFormatException, so find on its own is
answered the way every other incomplete command already is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Correct the Javadoc and cover every method
commitResults.messageBody:
Five weeks of moving code left comments describing an arrangement that
no longer exists. A comment that is merely absent costs a reader time. A
comment that is confidently wrong costs them trust in all the others,
so these were worth finding before adding any more.

mark, unmark and deleteTask each documented @throws TaskSaveException,
which none of them has declared since the parser was extracted and their
signatures widened to GudGoiException. The detail those lines carried,
that a change which cannot be saved is undone first, was folded into the
line that remains rather than dropped.

handle said the loop in main reads the lines. The loop moved to run when
the class gained a constructor.

Task told the reader that GudGoi.parseSavedTask reads the save form back
and reverses the escaping. Both moved to Storage two increments ago.

Let's also give the ten overriding methods in Todo, Deadline and Event a
header comment. The standard does not require one on an override, and
A-JavaDoc asks only for half of the non-private classes and methods. But
each of these adds something the parent cannot state: which letter the
type shows, which letter it stores, and which fields it appends. Every
non-private class and method in the project now carries a comment.

Nothing but comments changed, so there is no behaviour to compare. The
54 tests still pass, javadoc resolves every link, and the coding
standard check is clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Apply the peer review feedback and set up Checkstyle
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard is checked only by eye and by a helper script, so a
breach reaches the repository and is found later, by a reader. The peer
review on my pull request found several: British spellings in comments,
Javadoc summaries with no closing period, a boolean field named marked
rather than isMarked, and a command loop that hid an assignment inside
its while condition.

Let's put the standard into the build. Checkstyle now runs as part of
gradlew build, against the configuration the course publishes for the
intermediate standard, so a breach fails the build instead of waiting
for a reader to notice it.

Fixing what it reported touched most files, but no method body changed:
the edits are to names, comments and indents. The one design change is
Task, which becomes abstract with a protected constructor. Nothing ever
needs a plain Task, because every real task is a todo, a deadline or an
event, and the class cannot describe itself.

The two helper scripts learn the same lessons, so that the next commit
is checked for these breaches before Checkstyle sees it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a window, and keep the console
commitResults.messageBody:
The bot speaks only through a terminal. Level-10 asks for a graphical
window instead.

The commands are worth keeping exactly as they are, so the window is a
second front end rather than a rewrite. Let's have GudGoi's command
methods return their answer instead of printing it: run wraps that in
Ui.show, and the window puts the same text into a chat bubble. Neither
front end can drift from the other, because both go through handle.

Four new methods are the whole of what the window needs. getGreeting
and loadTasks open the session in the order the console already uses,
getResponse answers one line, and isExit says when to close.
getResponse returns a GudGoiException's message as ordinary text,
because a window has nowhere else to put an error.

The console stays. GudGoi.main is untouched, so the old session still
runs with java -cp build/libs/gudgoi.jar gudgoi.GudGoi. mainClass now
names the launcher, because the window is what the JAR should start.

JavaFX is bundled for Windows, macOS and Linux, so the one shadow JAR
runs on whichever machine marks it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Let Ui.show take a line for each argument
commitResults.messageBody:
Ui.show takes one string and splits it at every newline, so a caller
that holds a response in parts has to join the parts first. That
joining is a chain of concatenations spread over several lines, which
reads worse than the text it produces.

Let's make the parameter variable arity. A call that passes one built
string compiles unchanged and prints the same characters, because each
part is still broken at its own newline; a caller that holds parts can
now hand them over as they are.

The inner split stays, for a second reason. Every line goes to println
on its own, so the separator between lines is the one this system
uses. Printing a whole string in one call would leave a newline inside
it exactly as it was written, which is wrong on a system whose lines
end another way.

Nothing passes more than one part yet. Every command method returns a
single string, because getResponse has to give the window one. This
widens what Ui accepts; it does not change what GudGoi sends.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

When a TaskSaveException occurs after a command, the 'tasks' list is
restored to the state before the command. Nothing checked that this
undo worked, and a failed undo would write the wrong list to disk with
no error shown. Ensure that the task count, and the marked state, are
consistent with the previous state.

TaskList.insert and removeLast state their preconditions in Javadoc
only. Assert them instead. removeLast no longer ignores an empty
agenda, because that guard hid such a mistake instead of preventing it.

In parseCommandWord and parseArguments, ensure that prior trimming is
done by the caller. An untrimmed line makes the command word empty, so
every command would look unknown to the user.

Assertions are used rather than exceptions because no user input can
cause any of these. Input is still validated with checked exceptions.

Enable assertions on the test and run tasks, since the JVM ignores
assert statements without -ea. The TaskList test for the old removeLast
behaviour now expects the assertion, so it also fails if -ea is removed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The code follows the coding standard, and Checkstyle passes, but several
of the guidelines in the course code quality chapter are judgement
calls that no tool can check. Four of them are breached.

MainWindow.start is 51 lines and works at three levels of abstraction
at once: it creates controls, places them by pixel, wires event
handlers, and starts the session. Split it into layOutWindow,
wireHandlers and startSession, so the reader sees the four steps before
the detail of any one of them. Its controls are also created inside
start although they are fields. Initialize them where they are
declared, which lets them be final.

Storage.parseSavedTask is 37 lines and reads the split line through
bare indices. fields[3] means the due time in one branch and the start
time in another, and nothing says so. Name the field positions and the
per-type field counts, and give each task type its own builder, so no
arm of the switch carries a nested conditional.

The sentence that reports the running total is written twice in GudGoi,
and the two had drifted: an add says "1 task" while a delete says
"1 task(s)". Extract describeTotal so there is one wording. A third
copy of the pluralisation rule stays in OutOfBoundException, because it
is a different sentence in a different package and sharing it would
need a public helper class for one conditional.

Task.getTypeIcon and getTypeLetter return an empty string that no task
ever uses, since Task is abstract and all three subclasses override
both. Make them abstract, so the compiler asks a new subclass for an
answer instead of letting it inherit one that is wrong.

The duplication between listTasks and findTasks is left alone. The
A-Streams increment rewrites both methods and removes it as a side
effect, so doing it here would only create a conflict to throw away.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Three loops in this program exist only to turn one collection into
another shape. Written as loops, each one spends most of its lines on
the mechanics of iterating, and the reader has to run the loop in their
head to see what comes out.

listTasks and findTasks were near duplicates: the same index
arithmetic, the same numbering, the same separator handling, differing
only by a filter. Replace both bodies with calls to numberMatching,
which takes the filter as a Predicate and returns the numbered block.

numberMatching streams over positions rather than over the tasks. This
matters and is not a style choice: after a filter, the first task left
is no longer the first task in the agenda, so a stream of tasks would
number find's results 1, 2, 3 while mark still expects the real
positions. IntStream.range keeps the position and the task together.

In Storage.save, each task already knows how to write itself, so the
file is that one method applied down the list. In Ui.show, flatMap is
what turns "some parts, each holding some lines" into one run of lines.
split is kept over String.lines() there because the two differ on an
empty part, which would silently drop a blank line.

Storage.load keeps its loop. It has to stop at the first line it cannot
read and raise a checked Exception carrying that line, and a stream
expresses neither of those well.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Branch a streams
